sub_tasks.requirements: The context-calibration spec-centered formulation (fspec, fcode, fcheck, repair loop R) with Contraction and Expansion strategies for the two hallucination types (fabrication-by-extrapolation and fabrication-by-omission) is implemented as described.

The two hallucination types are correctly distinguished in the implementation: fabrication-by-extrapolation (the model extends partial evidence beyond what the paper supports, e.g. inventing an extra routing API or hyperparameter not specified for a mentioned adapter module) and fabrication-by-omission (the model fills an unspecified implementation choice with its own default, e.g. silently choosing a learning rate instead of flagging it as an unresolved gap).

The specification-generation function S = f_spec(P) is implemented, producing a structured implementation specification S from research paper P that contains the model architecture, loss functions, training procedures, hyperparameters, and other implementation-critical details, serving as the implementation contract for downstream stages.

The Expansion strategy is implemented within f_spec to reduce fabrication-by-omission: the system identifies information gaps in the paper (unspecified implementation details) and resolves them against external registries and citation APIs when needed, grounding S in paper evidence and trusted external sources rather than LLM intuition.
The code-generation function C_0 = f_code(S) is implemented, producing an initial codebase C_0 from the implementation specification S.

The Contraction strategy is implemented within f_code to reduce fabrication-by-extrapolation: the context provided to the model for generating each module is bounded strictly to the specifications and dependencies defined in S, preventing the model from inventing symbols or interfaces outside the established contract.

The check-construction function Q = f_check(S) = {q_i}_{i=1}^m is implemented such that executable checks (unit tests, static analysis, or artifact-level checks) are derived directly from the specification S rather than from the generated code, so validation is independent of the code-generation process.

Each check q_i is implemented to either pass or return a diagnostic when run against a codebase C_t, and at repair step t the set of failing diagnostics D_t = {q_i(C_t) : q_i(C_t) fails} is correctly collected.

The iterative repair loop is implemented such that if D_t is non-empty, a repair agent R updates the code via C_{t+1} = R(C_t, D_t, S), using the current codebase, the failing diagnostics, and the specification S as inputs.
The acceptance condition is implemented such that if D_t is empty at any repair step, the codebase C_t is accepted immediately without further repair iterations.
The final output C* is defined and produced as the first codebase in the repair loop for which all spec-derived checks pass, i.e. q_i(C*) = pass for all i in {1,...,m}.

The implementation maintains the three distinct roles described: the paper P provides evidence, the specification S defines the implementation contract, and the checks Q convert that contract into executable validation, such that C* must pass checks produced independently of the code-generation process (i.e., f_check operates on S, not on C_0 or C_t).

The implementation treats the raw research paper P strictly as an evidence source: all downstream artifacts (S, C_0, Q) must trace their content back to text, figures, tables, or appendices extracted from P, and no stage other than f_spec directly consumes the raw paper content to produce implementation-level artifacts.

The Partition Agent is the deterministic entry point that consumes the raw PDF-derived content list (MinerU *_content_list_v2.json) of paper P and produces role-tagged sections (body, appendix, references, preamble) plus an images list, verifying that raw paper content enters the pipeline only at this typed-substrate stage and not directly into later stages.

The Vision-Language Agent consumes figure images and captions extracted from paper P (via the partition stage's images key) and produces typed structured records (category, components, flows, stages, inputs, outputs) in figure_analysis, verifying that raw image content from P is only directly consumed by this stage and converted into a typed format before any other stage sees it.

The Gap Agent consumes the partitioned body and references/bibliography sections of paper P directly (per the Gap-Identification System Prompt) to extract reference metadata and identify the five categories of implementation gaps, verifying that gap analysis is grounded in text extracted from P rather than fabricated independently of the paper.

The goal-and-config extraction call within the Main Planning Agent consumes the partitioned sections of paper P directly to produce the goal_and_config markdown document, and the system prompt instructs the model not to fabricate values beyond what the paper explicitly provides, verifying this artifact traces to paper evidence.

The paper_analysis extraction call within the Main Planning Agent consumes the partitioned sections of paper P directly to extract equations, algorithms, figures/tables to reproduce, baselines, ablations, and datasets, verifying that paper_analysis traces to paper content rather than being independently invented by later stages.

The architecture-design call within the Main Planning Agent consumes only the already-extracted goal_and_config, paper_analysis, and figure_analysis artifacts (not the raw paper text/PDF directly) to produce the file-level architecture JSON, verifying that planning stages downstream of extraction consume S-derived artifacts rather than re-parsing raw paper content.

Each Sub-Planning Agent consumes the architecture, goal_and_config, paper_analysis, figure_analysis, the three independent plans, and module-relevant gaps (all S-derived artifacts) rather than the raw paper text, to produce per-file spec_text, verifying that module-level planning traces to the specification rather than to the raw paper.

The Code-Generation Agent (module and orchestrator passes) consumes only spec_text, architecture, goal_and_config, paper_analysis, review, relevant gaps, and previously generated source (all part of S or C_0), never the raw paper PDF or unpartitioned paper text directly, verifying that f_code implements strictly on S as required by the role-separation formulation.

The unit-test agent consumes previously generated source code, the AST-extracted symbol whitelist, and the codegen agent's LocalMemory trace, but does not directly consume the raw paper P, verifying that Q-generation traces to the specification/codebase rather than to re-reading paper content.

The Debug Agent consumes subprocess execution output, tracebacks, codebase file contents via read_file/search_codebase, and codegen LocalMemory, but does not directly consume the raw paper P, verifying that repair (R) operates on C_t, D_t, and S-derived context rather than re-deriving requirements from the paper text.

The specification-as-contract principle is correctly applied asymmetrically: module-file code-generation prompts receive the spec_text and source of only their declared dependencies, while orchestrator-file prompts receive the full source of every already-generated module in addition to the same S artifacts (architecture, goal_and_config, paper_analysis, review), reflecting the orchestrator's need to name symbols across the entire codebase versus a module's need to only match its declared neighborhood.

The module-file code-generation prompt includes the previously generated source code ONLY of files explicitly declared as dependencies for the current file in the architecture's dependencies list, and does not include the source of any other already-generated module file, implementing the Contraction principle at the code-generation stage.

The orchestrator-file code-generation prompt (for entry-point files and reproduce.sh) includes the full source code of every already-generated module file in the codebase, not just declared dependencies, reflecting the orchestrator's need to name symbols correctly across the entire codebase rather than only its declared neighborhood.

The code-generation agent implementation dispatches distinct context-assembly logic keyed on the orchestrator boolean flag from the architecture: files with orchestrator=true trigger the full-module-source assembly path, while files with orchestrator=false trigger the declared-dependency-only assembly path, verifying the asymmetric contraction/expansion split is driven mechanically by this flag rather than being ad hoc per file.

Code generation is implemented as two ordered passes: a first pass generating all non-orchestrator files in dependency order, and a second pass generating orchestrator files only after every module is on disk, ensuring the full-module-source context given to orchestrator prompts reflects realized generated code rather than only planned specs.

The checks Q = f_check(S) are implemented as executable validation artifacts (e.g., unit tests, static analysis via ast.parse, or artifact-level checks such as the debug agent's subprocess execution and liveness-token check) that convert the specification's contract into pass/fail signals, distinct from the code-generation process itself.

The implementation verifies that f_check is constructed as a function of S alone and NOT as a function of C_0 or any C_t: e.g., the debug agent's entry-point subprocess run and exit-code/liveness criteria are derived from the architecture's declared entry_point (part of S) rather than being inferred post-hoc by inspecting the generated code's internal structure, ensuring q_i(C*) validation is independent of how C* was produced.

The paper's claim that decoupling the contract (S) from the implementation (C*) reduces the probability of producing plausible-looking but non-functional code is reflected in the system design: checks Q must be satisfiable only by a codebase that actually implements the contract's requirements, not by a codebase that merely appears well-formed, as evidenced by the debug loop's requirement that q_i(C*) = pass for all i before the pipeline terminates successfully.

The implementation verifies that spec-derived checks q_i are constructed to test whether the contract's requirements are actually implemented (e.g., artifact-level checks that inspect subprocess exit codes and liveness tokens from real execution, or unit tests that exercise tensor shapes/values from actual forward passes), such that a codebase which merely contains syntactically well-formed but functionally incorrect or stubbed code would fail at least one q_i rather than passing checks trivially.

The implementation ensures checks are not satisfiable merely by superficial code well-formedness: ast.parse-based syntax validation during code generation is treated only as a necessary precondition (parseability), not as a sufficient check standing in for q_i, and semantic/behavioral correctness is instead validated separately at the debug stage via actual subprocess execution against the entry point declared in the architecture.

The debug loop is implemented such that it terminates in success only when every check q_i(C_t) passes for all i (i.e., the failing-diagnostics set D_t is empty), matching the formal acceptance criterion q_i(C*) = pass for all i; the loop must not terminate successfully while any q_i still fails, and must instead continue iterating (up to the max_iterations cap) via the repair agent R.

The debug agent's exit-code-zero-or-liveness-token criterion (a case-insensitive regex match for one of epoch, step, iter(ation), batch, loss, or train(ing) adjacent to a digit within the 120-second timeout) is implemented as evidence that the codebase reached genuine functional execution (e.g., entered the training loop) rather than merely appearing complete at the source level, distinguishing a functionally-progressing run from one that hangs in import, deadlocks during dataset construction, or stalls inside an empty loop.

The repair agent R is implemented to consume the actual failing diagnostics D_t (e.g., parsed tracebacks, crash file, line number) and produce a fix targeted at the root cause of functional failure via the submit_fix tool (edits, file_rewrites, or files_to_create), rather than applying cosmetic changes that would make the codebase appear plausible without resolving the underlying q_i failure, reflected in the debug system prompt's instruction to 'fix the RIGHT file' where the bug originates rather than only the file that crashed.

The Crafter system architecture of eight agent types (runtime 8+N instances) with the shared GlobalMemory key-value store and per-agent LocalMemory is implemented, including the fixed inter-agent dataflow and re-runnable-in-isolation stages.

The system is organized as exactly eight specialized agent types (Partition Agent, Vision-Language Agent, Gap Agent, Main Planning Agent, Sub-Planning Agent, Code-Generation Agent, Unit-Test Agent, Debug Agent), with Sub-Planning Agent instantiated once per code module such that the total runtime instance count for an architecture with N modules is 8 + N, as stated in Appendix B.1.

A GlobalMemory object is implemented as a stage-indexed key-value store instantiated once in run_pipeline and threaded into every agent at construction, serving as the single source of truth and the only channel through which agents communicate (agents do not call each other directly, return values to a coordinator, or pass arguments to each other).

GlobalMemory keys are namespaced by stage of origin as described in Appendix B.5: partitions and images from partitioning; figure_analysis from the vision-language stage; supplementary_context from the gap stage; architecture, goal_and_config, paper_analysis, experiment_plan, baseline_plan, dataset_plan, module_specs, and review from planning; generated_code and generated_tests from code generation and unit-test generation. Each agent reads its inputs from a fixed set of named keys and writes outputs back to the same store, with the consumer of each key determined statically.

GlobalMemory is persisted on disk as one file per key, serialized as JSON for structured values (lists, dicts, the architecture, the generated source map) and as Markdown for free-text values (the goal-and-config document, the three independent plans, the review), so that a partial state survives a process crash and individual keys can be inspected as flat-file reads.

GlobalMemory writes are implemented to be safe against concurrent puts from sub-agents running under asyncio.gather: the calling task serializes the value to a string in the asyncio thread first, then spawns a daemon thread that acquires a per-store lock and writes the immutable string to disk, ensuring the writer thread never observes a mutating object and that concurrent writes to different keys cannot interleave their bytes.

The GlobalMemory write path is implemented such that the calling asyncio task (not a background thread) first serializes the value to a string immediately upon put, choosing JSON encoding for structured values and Markdown for free-text values, before any thread boundary is crossed, ensuring the writer thread never observes a mutating Python object.

After serialization, the calling task spawns a daemon background thread to perform the actual disk write of the immutable string, so that the asyncio event loop is not blocked by file I/O and multiple concurrent puts from sub-agents running under asyncio.gather each dispatch to their own writer thread.

Each daemon writer thread acquires a per-store lock (scoped to the GlobalMemory store, not a single global lock across unrelated stores) before writing to disk and holds the lock for the duration of the I/O operation, so that two concurrent writes to different keys within the same store cannot interleave their bytes on disk.

The combined write pattern (serialize-then-spawn-locked-writer) is verified to be safe specifically under the pipeline's asyncio.gather-based concurrency (e.g. the N parallel Sub-Planning Agents in the planning stage, or the parallel goal-and-config/paper-analysis extraction calls), such that concurrent GlobalMemory.set calls from these fan-outs do not corrupt or interleave the on-disk file-per-key representation.

Each agent maintains its own LocalMemory containing three fields populated through helper methods inherited from the base agent: conversation_history, reasoning_trace, and intermediate_attempts, recording the agent's private reasoning and intermediate attempts, and uses the same async-safe write pattern as GlobalMemory but is per-agent rather than shared.

The LocalMemory implementation includes a conversation_history field that records the full message/turn history of the owning agent's LLM interactions, populated through a helper method inherited from the base agent class rather than being managed ad hoc by each agent subclass.

The LocalMemory implementation includes a reasoning_trace field that records the owning agent's intermediate reasoning steps (e.g. analysis text produced before a final decision or tool call), populated through a helper method inherited from the base agent class.

The LocalMemory implementation includes an intermediate_attempts field that records prior candidate outputs or attempts produced by the owning agent before its final accepted output (e.g. a rejected code draft or a failed fix proposal), populated through a helper method inherited from the base agent class.

All three LocalMemory fields (conversation_history, reasoning_trace, intermediate_attempts) are populated via helper methods defined once in a common base agent class and inherited by every agent subclass, rather than each agent type implementing its own separate logging mechanism, ensuring consistent LocalMemory population behavior across all eight agent types.

LocalMemory is implemented as a private, per-agent-instance store (one LocalMemory object per agent instance, including per-module Sub-Planning Agent instances and per-file Code-Generation Agent invocations) rather than a single shared store, distinguishing it structurally from the single shared GlobalMemory object.

LocalMemory writes use the same async-safe write pattern as GlobalMemory: the calling asyncio task serializes the value to a string before crossing the thread boundary, and a background daemon thread performs the actual disk write while holding a lock scoped to that LocalMemory instance, preventing corruption when the owning agent's coroutine and its writer thread interact concurrently.

The LocalMemory write path is implemented such that the owning agent's calling asyncio task serializes the value (conversation_history, reasoning_trace, or intermediate_attempts entries) to a string immediately upon write, before any thread boundary is crossed, matching the same serialize-before-dispatch pattern used by GlobalMemory as described in Appendix B.5.

After serialization, the calling task spawns a background daemon thread that performs the actual LocalMemory disk write, so that the owning agent's asyncio event loop is not blocked by file I/O during recording of its private trace.

Each LocalMemory daemon writer thread acquires a lock scoped specifically to that LocalMemory instance (not the shared GlobalMemory lock and not a single process-wide lock), and holds it for the duration of the write, preventing corruption when the owning agent's coroutine and its own writer thread interact concurrently.

The LocalMemory write implementation is verified to reuse the identical serialize-then-spawn-locked-writer pattern used by GlobalMemory (per Appendix B.5), differing only in that the lock and file target are scoped to the individual LocalMemory instance rather than the shared store, confirming the paper's claim that 'LocalMemory uses the same write pattern as GlobalMemory but is per-agent rather than shared.'

Each agent's LocalMemory trace is persisted to disk as a readable artifact (alongside GlobalMemory's file-per-key layout) so that, after a pipeline run completes, the LocalMemory of any agent instance is available for post-hoc analysis of agent behavior, independent of whether that trace was consumed by another agent during the run.

LocalMemory is private by convention and is read outside its owning agent in only two places: the unit-test agent loads the codegen LocalMemory of each file to recover the spec it was written against, and the debug agent reads codegen LocalMemory to reconstruct the rationale behind a particular generated file when diagnosing a failure; in every other case LocalMemory is write-only from the owning agent's perspective.

The pipeline enforces a fixed inter-agent dataflow mediated entirely by GlobalMemory rather than unstructured dialogue between agents (unlike prior multi-agent systems such as ChatDev and AutoGen): no agent invokes another agent's methods directly, and all information transfer between stages occurs by one agent writing to a named GlobalMemory key and a later agent reading that same key.

Because GlobalMemory keys are decoupled and statically consumed, individual pipeline stages are re-runnable in isolation: for example, invoking the debug agent against an existing run only requires that generated_code and architecture are populated in GlobalMemory, regardless of which other stages have executed in the current process, and every stage that finds its expected output keys already populated skips itself.

The implementation verifies that each pipeline stage's set of consumed GlobalMemory keys is statically determined by the stage's code (fixed named keys read from the store) rather than dynamically discovered or dependent on runtime coordination with other agents, so that any stage's input requirements can be enumerated without executing the full pipeline.

The debug agent can be invoked in isolation against an existing run by pointing a new pipeline invocation at the same output directory, requiring only that the generated_code and architecture GlobalMemory keys are already populated, regardless of whether partitioning, VLM analysis, gap analysis, planning, or unit-test generation have executed in the current process.

Every pipeline stage checks whether its expected output keys are already populated in GlobalMemory at the start of its execution and skips its own computation (LLM calls and side effects) if so, so that re-invoking run_pipeline against an existing output directory does not redundantly regenerate artifacts that already exist on disk.

The unit-test generation stage specifically implements the skip behavior described in Appendix B.3.6: if all expected test file paths already exist on disk under codebase/tests/, the stage skips itself entirely, making it cheap to re-invoke after a partial run.

The unit-test generation stage computes the expected set of test file paths as one tests/test_<module>.py per non-test, non-__init__ Python file in the generated codebase, prior to checking whether generation should be skipped, matching the description in Appendix B.3.6 that the stage 'produces one tests/test_<module>.py per non-test, non-__init__ Python file in the codebase.'

The unit-test generation stage checks, for every expected test file path derived from the codebase's source files, whether that exact path already exists on disk under codebase/tests/, before invoking any LLM call for test generation.

The unit-test generation stage implements the full self-skip behavior: if and only if all expected test file paths already exist on disk under codebase/tests/, the entire stage (including any per-file LocalMemory loading, symbol-whitelist construction, and LLM test-generation calls) is skipped, rather than performing a partial skip of only some files.

The unit-test generation stage's expected-test-path-existence check is implemented to run strictly before any other sub-stage work begins for the current invocation, so that when the all-paths-exist condition holds, no per-file LocalMemory loading, symbol-whitelist construction, or LLM test-generation call is triggered even transiently before the skip decision is made.

When the full-skip condition holds (all expected test file paths already exist under codebase/tests/), the unit-test agent does not load the codegen LocalMemory of any target file, verifying that LocalMemory loading is gated by the same all-or-nothing skip check rather than being performed unconditionally before the skip decision.

When the full-skip condition holds, the unit-test agent does not perform AST-based symbol-whitelist construction (walking previously generated files to extract importable top-level classes and functions) for any module, verifying that this step is skipped along with the rest of the stage rather than being computed and then discarded.

When the full-skip condition holds, no LLM test-generation call (using the Unit-Test Agent System Prompt) is issued for any file in the codebase, verifying that zero LLM invocations occur for the stage in this case, matching the claim that the stage is skipped 'making it cheap to re-invoke after a partial run.'

The skip logic is implemented as a single all-or-nothing decision over the full expected set of test file paths (skip entirely only if every path exists), rather than as an independent per-file skip check that could allow some files' LocalMemory loading, whitelist construction, or LLM calls to run while others are skipped within the same invocation.

Re-invoking the unit-test generation stage (e.g. via the --unit-test CLI flag) against an output directory where every expected tests/test_<module>.py file was already successfully written in a prior invocation is verified to produce zero additional LocalMemory reads, zero AST whitelist computations, and zero LLM calls, confirming the full self-skip behavior end-to-end rather than only at the unit level.

If at least one expected test file path is missing from disk under codebase/tests/, the unit-test generation stage does not skip entirely but proceeds to generate the missing test files (using the AST-extracted symbol whitelist and codegen LocalMemory as described elsewhere in Appendix B.3.6), verifying the skip condition is an all-or-nothing check over the full expected set rather than a per-file skip.

The self-skip behavior is verified to make the unit-test stage cheap to re-invoke after a partial pipeline run: re-running the pipeline (or the --unit-test flag in isolation) against an output directory where all test files were already successfully generated in a prior invocation incurs no additional LLM calls for that stage, consistent with the paper's claim that this 'makes it cheap to re-invoke after a partial run.'

The batch runner and pipeline CLI expose stage-skipping flags (--no-vlm, --skip-debug, --skip-gaps, --only-debug, --unit-test) that guard the corresponding awaits in run_pipeline, enabling partial-pipeline configurations such as the four-stage variant used with --skip-debug and the debug-only invocation used with --only-debug referenced in Appendix B.6.

The file-per-key on-disk layout of GlobalMemory (described in Appendix B.5) is verified to enable partial-state recovery after a process crash: a fresh run targeting the same output directory can reload any subset of previously written keys and either re-run only the failed stage in isolation or let cached upstream stages flow through unchanged.

All pipeline stages are implemented: structured partitioning, VLM figure analysis, gap analysis with external resolution, hierarchical planning with constraint validation and cross-module review, execution-aware code generation, unit-test generation, and the debug loop.

The Partition Agent stage is implemented: it is the only stage with no LLM call, consuming a MinerU-produced *_content_list_v2.json where the paper is already OCR'd and segmented into typed items (title, paragraph, equation_interline, algorithm, table, image, list, page_header, page_number), flattening this into a single item stream, dropping page_header and page_number items, and splitting the stream into sections at every title item with text_level == 1, tagging each section with a section_role from {body, appendix, references, preamble} via regex over the title text, and writing 'partitions' (role-tagged sections) and 'images' (figure entries) to GlobalMemory.

The Partition Agent stage is implemented such that it makes zero LLM calls, being purely deterministic parsing and regex-based logic operating on the MinerU content list, distinguishing it from all other pipeline stages that invoke an LLM.

The Partition Agent reads a MinerU-produced *_content_list_v2.json file for the paper, where the paper is already OCR'd and segmented into typed items with types including title, paragraph, equation_interline, algorithm, table, image, list, page_header, and page_number, verifying that the agent's input parser handles each of these listed item types.
The Partition Agent reads a MinerU-produced *_content_list_v2.json file for the paper, where the paper is already OCR'd and segmented into a list of pages, each a list of typed items.

The Partition Agent's input parser correctly handles each of the MinerU item types present in the content list: title, paragraph, equation_interline, algorithm, table, image, list, page_header, and page_number.

The Partition Agent flattens the nested MinerU content list into a single ordered stream of typed items, preserving the original document order across pages, so downstream section-splitting can operate on a single linear sequence rather than a page-nested structure.

The Partition Agent drops all page_header and page_number typed items from the flattened stream before section splitting, ensuring these items never appear in any output section or in the 'partitions' GlobalMemory value.

The Partition Agent splits the flattened item stream into sections at every title item whose text_level field equals 1, such that each resulting section begins with one top-level title item and includes all subsequent items up to (but not including) the next text_level == 1 title item.

The Partition Agent tags each split section with a section_role value drawn from the fixed set {body, appendix, references, preamble}, determined by applying regex matching over the title text of that section (e.g. matching 'appendix' or 'supplementary' patterns for appendix, 'references'/'bibliography' patterns for references, and treating pre-title content or abstract/front-matter as preamble, with all remaining sections defaulting to body).

The Partition Agent writes the role-tagged sections (each section's items plus its assigned section_role) to the 'partitions' key in GlobalMemory, matching the GlobalMemory key namespace described for the partitioning stage.

The Partition Agent extracts all image-typed items from the flattened stream (including their captions and any associated metadata) and writes them as figure entries to the 'images' key in GlobalMemory, which is later consumed by the Vision-Language Agent stage.

The Vision-Language Agent stage is implemented: for each image entry surfaced by the partition stage, it makes a classification call (excluding result_plot, example, other categories and retaining only architecture, pipeline, system_workflow, or algorithm figures) followed by a structured-extraction call (only on classified-in figures) that returns {category, extracted: {components, flows, stages, inputs, outputs}} using the exact VLM Classification Prompt and VLM Structured-Extraction Prompt text, writing results to figure_analysis in GlobalMemory without re-showing the original image to any later stage.

The Vision-Language Agent stage iterates over every image entry present in the 'images' key written to GlobalMemory by the Partition Agent stage, processing each figure independently rather than batching all figures into a single call.

For each image entry, the Vision-Language Agent implementation makes a classification LLM call first, and only proceeds to a structured-extraction call for that image if the classification call's returned category passes the retention filter, implementing the two-call sequential design.

The execution-oriented Probe-Plan-Run-Extract harness with milestone ladder (M0-M7), locked protocols, fixtures, metric extraction, and repair-audit protocol is implemented and run on LBCS, SEMA, and LCA-on-the-Line, reproducing the pre-repair milestones (Table 4), repair distances (Table 5), and final emitted metrics (Tables 12-15).

The three papers evaluated in the execution-oriented harness (LBCS, Self-Expansion/SEMA, LCA-on-the-Line) are selected from the 23-paper PaperBench subset according to the four criteria stated in Appendix D.1: contractable empirical claims, meaningful under fixture-scale execution (at most one epoch, roughly 10^3 samples), lightweight infrastructure requirements (no external LLM APIs, no specialized RL environments, no >1B parameter model downloads), and no safety-refusal confounds (excluding dual-use security papers).

Each of the three selected papers (LBCS, SEMA, LCA-on-the-Line) satisfies the 'contractable claim' selection criterion from Appendix D.1: its central empirical contribution can be expressed as a directional comparison between a method and a baseline metric, of the form metric_method >= metric_baseline (or the reverse direction for distance-like metrics), so that the harness can distinguish a repository that merely runs from one that reproduces the qualitative direction of the paper's main claim.

Each of the three selected papers satisfies the 'meaningful under fixture-scale execution' criterion from Appendix D.1: the paper's reduced experiment can run with at most one epoch and roughly 10^3 samples while still exercising a real computational path (not merely testing training duration), as verified by the fixture sizes described in Appendix D.3 (mnist_tiny with 1,000 images, cifar_multitask with five two-class tasks, gaussian_mixture with four-class hierarchical data).

Each of the three selected papers satisfies the 'lightweight infrastructure requirements' criterion from Appendix D.1: none of LBCS, SEMA, or LCA-on-the-Line require external LLM APIs, specialized reinforcement-learning environments, or downloads of models larger than 1B parameters, keeping all execution runs within a comparable single-GPU budget.

Each of the three selected papers satisfies the 'no safety-refusal confounds' criterion from Appendix D.1: none of LBCS, SEMA, or LCA-on-the-Line are dual-use security papers involving adversarial attacks, jailbreaks, or red-teaming, so that code-generation model safety-policy behavior does not become a confounder in the reproducibility evaluation.

LBCS is confirmed as one of the three selected papers, testing data-efficient learning via bilevel optimization and lexicographic coreset selection, as stated in Appendix D.1's description of the resulting subset spanning three different ML settings.

Self-Expansion (abbreviated SEMA following the authors) is confirmed as one of the three selected papers, testing continual learning with a frozen backbone, router, and dynamically expanding modular adapters, as stated in Appendix D.1.

LCA-on-the-Line is confirmed as one of the three selected papers, testing a semantic-distance evaluation mechanism (Lowest Common Ancestor distance) through the paper's controlled simulation phase, as stated in Appendix D.1.

The three papers selected for the execution-oriented evaluation (LBCS, SEMA, LCA-on-the-Line) are each members of the same 23-paper PaperBench subset used for the PaperBench Code-Dev evaluation in Section 4.1/Table 1, verifying no paper outside the 23-paper set is substituted into the execution-readiness evaluation.

The execution-oriented protocol for LCA-on-the-Line targets specifically Phase 1 (the controlled simulation phase) as described in Appendix D.1, following Appendix C of the original LCA-on-the-Line paper, rather than the larger benchmark phase across 75 pretrained vision models on ImageNet and OOD variants, since that scale exceeds the single-GPU smoke/pilot budget.

The execution milestone ladder M0-M7 from Table 3 is implemented in the harness with the exact criteria for each milestone level, used to score every generated repository's progress toward an executable, claim-bearing reproduction.

The harness implements milestone M0 exactly as defined in Table 3: 'No entry point discovered.' The harness's probe step must classify a repository as M0 when it cannot discover any executable entry point, CLI command, or launch mechanism during the probing phase, prior to attempting any smoke or pilot run.

The harness implements milestone M1 exactly as defined in Table 3: 'Entrypoint found, but did not launch or failed immediately.' The harness must classify a repository as M1 when an entry point is discovered during probing, but invoking it as a subprocess either fails to launch (e.g. immediate process-start error) or crashes immediately (e.g. on the first executed statements) before reaching the smoke run's substantive computation.

The harness implements milestone M2 exactly as defined in Table 3: 'Launched, but smoke run did not complete within timeout.' The harness must classify a repository as M2 when the discovered entry point launches successfully as a subprocess but the smoke run does not finish within the 600-second smoke timeout specified in Appendix D.2.

The harness implements milestone M3 exactly as defined in Table 3: 'Smoke run completed, but produced no nonempty artifact.' The harness must classify a repository as M3 when the smoke run finishes within the timeout, but the harness's artifact scan (per Appendix D.5, scanning results/, outputs/, logs/, checkpoints/, figures/, runs/, experiments/) finds no newly created nonempty output file.

The harness implements milestone M4 exactly as defined in Table 3: 'Smoke artifacts exist, but pilot run did not complete.' The harness must classify a repository as M4 when the smoke run produces at least one nonempty artifact, but the subsequent pilot run (launched per the locked protocol's pilot intent) does not complete within the 1800-second pilot timeout specified in Appendix D.2.

The harness implements milestone M5 exactly as defined in Table 3: 'Pilot run completed, but liveness predicate failed.' The harness must classify a repository as M5 when the pilot run completes within its timeout, but the M6 liveness predicate (the paper-specific finite, in-range metric keys from Table 2/Table 10) is not satisfied by the metrics the harness extracts from the pilot run's output.

The harness implements milestone M6 exactly as defined in Table 3: 'Liveness predicate passed, but contribution predicate failed.' The harness must classify a repository as M6 when the extracted pilot-run metrics satisfy the paper-specific liveness predicate (finite, in-range values for the required metric keys, e.g. acc_lbcs, train_loss for LBCS per Table 2/Table 10) but fail to satisfy the M7 contribution-direction predicate (e.g. acc_lbcs > acc_uniform).

The harness implements milestone M7 exactly as defined in Table 3: 'Contribution predicate passed.' The harness must classify a repository as M7 when the extracted pilot-run metrics satisfy both the M6 liveness predicate and the paper-specific qualitative contribution-direction invariant from Table 2/Table 10 (e.g. acc_lbcs > acc_uniform for LBCS, acc_sema > acc_baseline for SEMA, lca_method < lca_baseline for LCA-on-the-Line), representing the deepest milestone indicating an executable, claim-bearing reproduction.

The harness implements the milestone ladder as a strictly ordered, monotonically increasing sequence M0 < M1 < M2 < M3 < M4 < M5 < M6 < M7, such that each milestone's criterion is checked only after all preceding milestones' criteria have been satisfied, and a repository is assigned the highest milestone level whose criterion it satisfies (per Table 3's description: 'Higher milestones indicate deeper progress toward an executable, claim-bearing reproduction').

The identical M0-M7 milestone-ladder predicate implementation is applied uniformly by the harness to score generated repositories from all three compared methods (Crafter, Paper2Code, DeepCode), with no method-specific relaxation or tightening of any milestone criterion, ensuring the pre-repair milestone assignments reported in Table 4 and the repair-audit records in Table 15 are computed under a single shared scoring function.

For each of the three papers (LBCS, SEMA, LCA-on-the-Line), a locked, paper-side, method-neutral execution protocol is authored before evaluating any generated repository, containing a smoke intent, a pilot intent, a timeout budget (600s smoke / 1800s pilot), and a layered success predicate (M6 liveness + M7 contribution), matching Appendix D.2 and the specific intents in Table 9.

Deterministic fixture families are constructed and shared identically across all evaluated methods: mnist_tiny (1,000 MNIST images, flat NPZ and torchvision-compatible MNIST format) for LBCS, cifar_multitask (five two-class tasks sampled from CIFAR-100, ImageFolder-style) for SEMA, and gaussian_mixture (four-class hierarchical Gaussian data with ID/OOD splits and a two-level hierarchy file) for LCA-on-the-Line, supplied to the repository only via environment variables (MNIST_PATH, CIFAR_MULTITASK_PATH, GAUSSIAN_MIX_PATH, HIERARCHY_FILE), as described in Appendix D.3.

The method-neutral Probe-Plan-Run-Extract harness is implemented as described in Appendix D.4: it probes the generated repository to discover entry points/CLI flags/env vars/config files, a fixed auxiliary planner emits a JSON invocation plan for smoke and pilot runs validated against the discovered interface (rejecting fabricated flags, unknown env vars, unregistered fixtures), runs the repository as a direct subprocess without a shell wrapper, and scans newly written JSON artifacts to compute the evaluated metrics.json itself.

Metric extraction is performed exclusively by the harness (not the repository or planner) as described in Appendix D.5: JSON files under standard output directories (results/, outputs/, logs/, checkpoints/, figures/, runs/, experiments/) are scanned, leaf keys flattened and matched against protocol-declared regex aliases, with a fixed LLM mapper proposing a dotted JSON path only accepted if it resolves to a finite scalar, and the final M6/M7 predicates per paper (Table 10) are evaluated over these harness-extracted metrics.

The bounded repair loop (20-cycle cap) and repair-tier taxonomy from Appendix D.6/Table 11 are implemented: each cycle records observed failure, automatically-classified root-cause category via regex rules over stdout/stderr (syntax errors, missing imports, undefined symbols, function-signature mismatches, missing files/configs, dependency errors, CLI mismatches, tensor/device/dtype errors, timeouts, OOM failures, invalid outputs), patch description, files edited, and line delta, plus a manually-assigned severity tier (S1 mechanical surface fixes, S2 localized logic/config fixes, S3 architectural gaps).
